headline: A natively signed C509 certificate is refused when it spells an algorithm generically instead of using the registry entry that names the same value.
summary:
Section 3.7 of the C509 draft requires a natively signed certificate to use only the specific CBOR encoding: where a registry entry exists for a value, the certificate carries the entry's integer rather than the OID form. The same section keeps the generic form available when decoding a re-encoded X.509 certificate, which may have been produced before the specific encoding was registered. The decoder applied neither half, accepting the generic form for any certificate type. It now refuses it on a natively signed certificate and continues to accept it on a re-encoded one.

The rule matches on the value, not the shape. A registry entry fixes both an OID and its parameters, so a generic spelling is the entry's value only when the parameters agree: an algorithm with no registry entry, or a registry OID carrying parameters the entry does not name, keeps the generic form and is still accepted. Encoding now selects its form by the same match, so re-encoding a parsed certificate field by field writes each algorithm back as the form that states the same value. An algorithm carrying no parameters is no longer moved to a registry entry that names some, and one whose parameters are an entry's own is written as that entry's integer however the caller identified it.

Separately, the type-3 reconstruction of an rsaEncryption public key emitted the OID and a NULL whatever the certificate carried, so supplied parameters were discarded and an algorithm identifier stating that it has none was rebuilt as though it had NULL. RFC 3279 section 2.3.1 fixes those parameters to NULL. The reconstruction now requires them and refuses both a different value and their absence, rather than rebuilding DER the certificate did not encode.

Added: The subjectPublicKeyAlgorithm on a pki.schema.c509.parse result carries a parameters buffer when the certificate used a C509 registry integer, holding the parameters that entry names: the DER NULL for rsaEncryption and the namedCurve OID for an EC key. The generic OID forms already surfaced this field, so it is now present for every form that has parameters.
Fixed: pki.schema.c509.parse refuses a natively signed certificate (c509CertificateType 2) that writes an algorithm as an OID, or as an OID with parameters, when a C509 registry entry names that same value. Draft section 3.7 reserves the generic form for re-encoded certificates, where it stays accepted. An algorithm with no registry entry, and a registry OID whose parameters differ from the entry's, both keep the generic form.

pki.schema.c509.parse refuses an rsaEncryption subjectPublicKeyAlgorithm that does not carry the DER NULL parameters RFC 3279 section 2.3.1 requires, including the bare OID form that carries none. The type-3 reconstruction previously emitted the OID and a NULL regardless, so the rebuilt DER described an algorithm identifier the certificate had not encoded.

pki.schema.c509.encode writes an algorithm back as the form naming the same value. It previously chose the form by algorithm name alone, so re-encoding a certificate field by field could move an algorithm that carried no parameters onto a registry entry that names some, and could miss the entry for a key identified by its namedCurve parameters rather than by a curve name.
